audience: undergraduate computer science; spoken explanation of 1-3 minutes

key_points.text: A deadlock is a state in which a set of processes or threads each wait for a resource held by another member of the set, so none of them can ever proceed.
key_points.partial_if: says processes are 'stuck' or 'waiting' without saying they wait on each other

key_points.text: All four (Coffman) conditions must hold at once: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.
key_points.partial_if: names some of the conditions, or all four without saying all must hold together

key_points.text: A concrete example, such as two threads that each hold one lock and request the lock the other holds.
key_points.partial_if: gives an example that is incomplete or not clearly a circular wait

key_points.text: Prevention: make one condition impossible, e.g. acquire locks in a fixed global order (no circular wait) or request all resources at once (no hold and wait).
key_points.partial_if: says deadlocks can be prevented but gives no mechanism

key_points.text: Avoidance and detection: avoid unsafe states (e.g. Banker's algorithm), or detect cycles in a wait-for graph and recover by aborting or preempting a process.
key_points.partial_if: mentions avoidance or detection by name only

misconceptions.text: Deadlock is the same as starvation, or simply a process that is slow or busy.
A deadlock resolves itself if the processes wait long enough.
Any single condition, such as mutual exclusion alone, is enough to cause a deadlock.
